Let It Ride Basics: Rules, Bonus Bets, and the House Edge

Published September 17, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Let It Ride markets itself on a promise most table games can't make: you're never actually betting against anyone, not the dealer, not the other players. It's a five-card poker hand scored against a fixed pay table, with a twist that makes it genuinely different from video poker — you get to look at part of your hand and pull money back before the rest is revealed. That pull-back mechanic is the entire game, and understanding it properly is the difference between playing close to the table's true house edge and giving up considerably more than you need to.

How a hand of Let It Ride is dealt

Each player makes three equal bets to start a hand — call them Bet 1, Bet 2, and Bet 3 — placed in three marked spots on the layout. Every player is dealt three cards, face down, dealt only to themselves; there's no dealer hand to compare against. Two additional community cards are placed face down in front of the dealer and used by every player at the table at the same time. The final hand each player is scored on is their three private cards plus those two shared community cards — a standard five-card poker hand.

The game unfolds in stages. Players look at their three private cards first and make a decision about Bet 1 before anything else is revealed. Then the dealer turns over the first community card, and players make a second decision about Bet 2. Finally the dealer turns over the second community card, completing the five-card hand, and the table settles up based on the pay table.

The three-bet structure, one decision at a time

At each of the first two decision points, a player either "lets it ride" — leaving that bet in action — or pulls it back, removing it from the table with no gain and no loss. Bet 3 always stays in action for the full hand; it's never eligible to be pulled back. That structure means a weak starting hand can be trimmed down to a single live bet before the community cards even finish revealing, capping the damage, while a strong hand can stay at all three bets, multiplying the eventual payout.

This is what separates Let It Ride from a straightforward wager: the player has real, informed control over how much money is exposed at each stage, based on partial information about their own hand. No other bet in the building works quite like it.

Worth remembering: pulling a bet back doesn't cost anything and doesn't forfeit a win — it simply removes that portion of your total stake from being multiplied by whatever the final hand pays.

Correct strategy: when to let it ride

Basic strategy for the first decision (with only your three private cards visible) is narrow and specific: let it ride if you already have a winning hand outright — a pair of 10s or better — or if your three cards are three to a royal flush (three cards, same suit, each ten or higher, in position to complete a royal). Every other three-card starting hand should be pulled back on Bet 1.

The second decision, after the first community card is revealed, expands slightly because you now have four of your five cards. Let it ride if you already have a made winning hand (pair of 10s or better), if you have four cards to a flush, or if you have four cards to an open-ended straight. Anything short of those situations should be pulled back on Bet 2, even if the hand still has some chance to improve on the final card — the odds at that point don't favor leaving the second bet exposed.

These rules are simple enough to memorize completely in a few minutes, and unlike more complex table games, there's no meaningful "close call" territory that requires a full strategy chart — the decision points are binary and the thresholds are clean.

A worked example

Say a player is dealt jack-jack-9, three different suits. That's a pair of jacks — already a winning hand on the base pay table — so Bet 1 stays in action. The dealer turns the first community card: a 4. The hand is still just a pair of jacks, no improvement, but it's still a made winning hand, so Bet 2 also stays in. The dealer turns the final community card: another jack, making three jacks. The final hand — three jacks plus a 4 and a 9 — pays at the three-of-a-kind rate on the pay table, and because all three original bets stayed in play, that payout applies to the full three-unit stake rather than just one unit.

Compare that to a player dealt 7-3-2 off-suit — nothing close to a made hand and no realistic straight or flush draw. Correct strategy pulls Bet 1 back immediately, leaving only Bet 3 exposed for the rest of the hand regardless of what the community cards turn out to be. That single decision is what keeps a genuinely bad starting hand from compounding into a bigger loss.

The pay table and house edge

HandTypical payout
Royal flush1,000 to 1
Straight flush200 to 1
Four of a kind50 to 1
Full house11 to 1
Flush8 to 1
Straight5 to 1
Three of a kind3 to 1
Two pair2 to 1
Pair of 10s or better1 to 1

Played with correct strategy, Let It Ride carries a house edge of roughly 3.5%, calculated against the total amount put into action across all three bets. That places it above blackjack played with correct basic strategy and a shade above Three Card Poker's base game, but still well inside the range of a reasonably player-friendly table game, and far better than a game like keno. As with any pay-table game, the exact numbers above vary by casino — some properties post slightly lower payouts on the middle tiers of the table, which raises the house edge, so it's worth glancing at the posted pay table before sitting down.

The Bonus side bet

Most Let It Ride tables offer an optional Bonus bet, made separately from the three main bets, before the hand starts. It pays out purely on the strength of the player's final five-card hand — win or lose on the main game is irrelevant to it — typically starting with a small payout for a pair of jacks or better in some versions, or scaling from three of a kind upward in others, and running up to a large fixed jackpot or a progressive jackpot for a royal flush at some properties.

The Bonus bet's house edge tends to run noticeably higher than the base game's, often somewhere in the mid-to-high single digits or beyond depending on the specific pay table and whether a progressive jackpot is attached. It's a legitimate, transparent side wager, but it isn't a "free roll" on money you were already putting into the base game — it's a separate bet with its own, generally worse, math, similar in spirit to the side bets covered in our blackjack side bets guide.

Common mistakes

The most common mistake is letting a bet ride out of hope rather than by the rule — leaving Bet 1 in on a hand like king-9-4 because "you never know," when correct strategy calls for pulling it back every time. A second is misjudging a four-card straight draw as open-ended when it isn't; only an open-ended draw (one that can complete on either end) qualifies for letting Bet 2 ride, not an inside draw that needs one specific rank. A third is treating the Bonus bet as low-risk because the wager itself is usually small relative to the main bets, without accounting for how much higher its house edge typically runs. And a fourth is assuming every casino's pay table is identical — the mid-tier payouts (flush, straight, three of a kind) are exactly the numbers that shift most between properties, and they matter more to your long-run result than the eye-catching royal flush jackpot at the top.

Frequently asked questions

Can Bet 3 ever be pulled back?

No. Bet 3 stays in action for the entire hand regardless of what the player's cards show. Only Bet 1 and Bet 2 can be withdrawn, and only at their respective decision points.

Is Let It Ride a form of poker against the house?

Not in the usual sense. There's no dealer hand to beat — every player's five-card hand is scored independently against a fixed pay table, so one player's result has no bearing on another's.

Does it matter what other players at the table do with their bets?

No. Every player uses the same two community cards but holds separate private cards, and every hand is paid independently off the pay table. Other players' decisions have no effect on your payout.

Is the Bonus bet ever worth making?

It comes down to personal risk preference. Its house edge is generally worse than the base game's, but it also offers a shot at a large fixed or progressive jackpot for a small, separate wager — the same tradeoff that applies to most jackpot-style side bets across the casino floor.
